question: In infants and young children, what is the main way the body keeps up cardiac output?
explanation: A child's heart has a limited ability to pump more blood per beat, so it relies heavily on beating faster to increase cardiac output. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why does a baby's large back of the head (occiput) make opening the airway tricky during resuscitation?

options.A: It narrows the internal jugular veins
options.B: It completely blocks the nasal passages
options.C: It forces the neck into passive flexion

explanation: An infant's prominent head causes their neck to bend forward when they lie flat on their back, which can easily block their soft airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h1)

question: When using the Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT), which side looks at brain function and mental alertness?
explanation: Appearance reflects how well the central nervous system is working, showing us the child's level of alertness and brain perfusion. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h2)

question: A toddler has nasal flaring and pulls in their chest muscles when breathing, but is alert with a normal skin color. Which part of the PAT is mainly affected?
explanation: Nasal flaring and pulling in of chest muscles are classic warning signs that the child is working much harder than usual to breathe. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the right chest compression-to-breath ratio when two rescuers are doing CPR on a child?
explanation: When two people are performing CPR on a child, they use 15 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h3)

question: How deep should you press the chest when doing CPR on an infant?

options.A: At least one-third the depth of the chest
options.B: Exactly one inch regardless of body size
options.C: Two full inches to reach the heart chambers
options.D: Half the depth of the infant chest wall

explanation: Compressing the chest by at least one-third of its total front-to-back depth ensures blood circulates effectively during an arrest. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which method is the most reliable way to confirm a breathing tube (endotracheal tube) is in the right place?
explanation: Capnography detects exhaled carbon dioxide, which is the gold standard for proving the tube went into the trachea and not the stomach. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is a common problem when using a bag-valve-mask with too much force or pressure on a child?
explanation: Blowing air in too hard or fast forces air into the stomach instead of the lungs, which can lead to vomiting. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which breath sound points most clearly to an upper airway blockage in a child?
explanation: Stridor is a harsh, high-pitched sound heard when breathing in, usually caused by narrowing in the upper airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h5)

question: Why does respiratory failure often lead directly to cardiac arrest in children?

options.A: Hypoxia and hypercarbia directly depress the myocardium
options.B: Systemic blood pressure rises too fast to sustain output
options.C: Pulmonary infections always spread directly to the heart
options.D: Children have an inherently fragile heart muscle

explanation: Running out of oxygen and building up carbon dioxide weakens the heart muscle over time until it stops beating. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the standard first dose of IV fluid given to a child in hypovolemic shock?
explanation: A rapid fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg of isotonic solution is the standard starting treatment to replace lost volume. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h6)

question: A child comes in with early septic shock, warm skin, and strong, bounding pulses. How is this type of shock described?
explanation: Septic shock causes blood vessels to widen incorrectly, which often makes the skin feel warm at first. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h6)

question: What heart rhythm is most commonly seen when a child suffers cardiac arrest?
explanation: Unlike adults who frequently have shockable rhythms, children in cardiac arrest most often present with asystole or PEA. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the recommended starting shock dose when using a defibrillator on a child with ventricular fibrillation?
explanation: The initial manual shock dose for a shockable rhythm in a pediatric patient is 2 Joules per kilogram. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why should we avoid driving carbon dioxide levels too low with over-ventilation after resuscitating a child?

options.A: It rapidly destroys surfactant in damaged lung tissue
options.B: It prevents effective renal clearance of metabolic acids
options.C: It causes cerebral vasoconstriction and reduced brain perfusion
options.D: It immediately triggers malignant ventricular arrhythmias

explanation: Low carbon dioxide makes the blood vessels in the brain narrow down, which cuts off necessary blood flow after CPR. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h8)

question: What is a main goal for managing body temperature after a child is successfully resuscitated from cardiac arrest?

options.A: Maintaining core temperature above normal limits
options.B: Inducing mild hypothermia in all pediatric patients
options.C: Allowing natural febrile responses to clear pathogens
options.D: Preventing fever to protect against further brain injury

explanation: Fever puts extra stress on the brain when it is already recovering from lack of oxygen, so keeping the temperature normal is crucial. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h8)
